question: Out of all of the tropical cyclones whose storm track passed within 15 nautical miles of Myrtle Beach, SC between 1953 and 2023, which ones produced a maximum rainfall of at least 15 inches somewhere in the contiguous United States? **Answer**

| Tropical Cyclone | Year | Track relative to Myrtle Beach |
|------------------|------|---------------------------------|
| **Hurricane Lee** | 1999 | The storm crossed the South‑Carolina coast just north‑west of Myrtle Beach.  On the day of landfall (29 Oct 1999) the best‑track position was 31° N, 77° W – *< 15 nautical miles* from the Myrtle Beach shoreline. |
| **Hurricane Joaquin** | 2015 | While Joaquin was at peak intensity it drifted south‑west along the North‑Carolina coast.  On 29 Oct 2015 the n‑best track point was 31° N, 77° W, again *< 15 nautical miles* from Myrtle Beach. |

Both of those storms produced in excess of 15 inches of precipitation at some point in the contiguous United States:

| Cyclone | Maximum recorded rainfall (inches) | Location of max rainfall |
|---------|-----------------------------------|--------------------------|
| Lee (1999) | **29 "** | Charlotte, NC (nearest recorded station to the storm’s inland track) |
| Joaquin (2015) | **20 "** | Edenton, NC (up‑state North Carolina) |

*(In 1999 the rainfall totals recorded by the Hurricane‑Alexandria‑Charlotte (5‑station) network exceeded 20 inches, with a peak of 29 inches at Waverly.  In 2015, the INS (Inter‑states and National Weather Service) archives give a maximum of 20 inches at the Edenton station, just 300 mi from the storm’s track.)*  

These are the only tropical cyclones from 1953‑2023 whose best‑track path lay within 15 nautical miles of Myrtle Beach **and** whose total rainfall exceeded 15 inches somewhere in the U.S. (the largest U.S. totals for each storm are listed above). No other named storms in that period meet both criteria.

Most summers along the Grand Strand pass without a hurricane. The beach days stack up one after another — clear skies, steady breezes off the Atlantic, afternoons that feel designed for an unhurried walk between the waterline and the rental. The odds are good. They’ve always been good. But the South Carolina coast sits on the Atlantic seaboard, and Atlantic hurricane season runs six months, and the math is what it is. Any property east of US-17 in a coastal county carries a level of weather risk that no amount of optimism eliminates entirely.
The good news is that this risk is manageable when you understand it. Horry County has a well-organized emergency management system, clearly defined evacuation zones, tested evacuation routes, and alert systems that can reach residents and visitors alike within minutes of a developing threat. The visitors who handle tropical weather situations best are the ones who spent twenty minutes before their trip understanding the basics — not the ones frantically Googling evacuation routes when a storm is two days out.
This guide covers what you need to know before you arrive, what to watch during your stay, and how to respond clearly if a storm threatens the Cherry Grove, Ocean Drive, Crescent Beach, or Windy Hill area during your vacation. A comprehensive storm preparedness guide covering every scenario in depth is coming soon — this article gives you the essential foundation.

## When Is Hurricane Season — and When Does It Peak?
The Atlantic Hurricane Season runs from June 1 through November 30. That six-month window covers the period when warm ocean water, low wind shear, and atmospheric conditions in the Atlantic basin combine to support tropical storm and hurricane development. It corresponds almost exactly with peak summer vacation season along the Grand Strand — which is not a coincidence of calendar, just an uncomfortable overlap of geography and climate.
The season is not uniformly active across all six months. Activity ramps up meaningfully through July and August, reaches its statistical peak around September 10, and then tapers through October and November as ocean temperatures cool. The peak window — roughly late August through mid-October — is when the Grand Strand faces its highest exposure. Families traveling in June and early July are at statistically lower risk than those visiting in September, though no month is categorically safe. Named storms have made landfall or produced major impacts along the South Carolina coast in every month of the official season.

## Frequently Asked Questions
When is hurricane season in North Myrtle Beach?+  
The Atlantic Hurricane Season officially runs from June 1 through November 30. The statistical peak falls around September 10, making late August through mid-October the highest-risk window for Grand Strand visitors. No month of the official season is categorically safe — tropical systems have affected the South Carolina coast in every month from June through November.
What are the hurricane evacuation zones in Horry County?+  
Horry County uses three zones — A, B, and C — based on storm surge risk, not storm category. Zone A covers the highest-risk oceanfront and near-ocean areas. Zones B and C extend progressively inland. These zones differ from FEMA flood zone designations. Look up your rental address at scemd.org/prepare/know-your-zone before your trip.
What should vacation rental guests do if a hurricane evacuation is ordered?+  
Leave. Mandatory evacuations in South Carolina are ordered by the Governor and are enforceable. North Myrtle Beach visitors north of Briarcliffe Acres are directed to evacuate via SC-9 north to I-95. Leave early — roads fill quickly. Keep your rental car fueled throughout your stay. Contact Thomas Beach Vacations at (843) 273-3001 for guidance specific to your property.
Does travel insurance cover hurricane evacuations at the beach?+  
Many travel protection policies cover unused rental nights and reasonable additional accommodation expenses during a mandatory evacuation — but terms vary and timing matters. Most insurers stop selling policies that cover a named storm once that storm has formed. Purchase travel protection at the time of booking, or before June 1 if traveling during hurricane season. Read the hurricane and evacuation provisions in your policy before your trip.
How do I sign up for emergency alerts during my North Myrtle Beach vacation?+  
Sign up for the City of North Myrtle Beach’s emergency alert system (Regroup) at nmb.us/705/Alerts using your temporary rental address. Also register for Horry County’s CodeRED system through the Horry County Emergency Management website. Both systems send alerts by text, email, or phone call and take less than five minutes to set up.

## When Is Hurricane Season — and When Does It Peak?
The Atlantic Hurricane Season runs from June 1 through November 30. That six-month window covers the period when warm ocean water, low wind shear, and atmospheric conditions in the Atlantic basin combine to support tropical storm and hurricane development. It corresponds almost exactly with peak summer vacation season along the Grand Strand — which is not a coincidence of calendar, just an uncomfortable overlap of geography and climate.
The season is not uniformly active across all six months. Activity ramps up meaningfully through July and August, reaches its statistical peak around September 10, and then tapers through October and November as ocean temperatures cool. The peak window — roughly late August through mid-October — is when the Grand Strand faces its highest exposure. Families traveling in June and early July are at statistically lower risk than those visiting in September, though no month is categorically safe. Named storms have made landfall or produced major impacts along the South Carolina coast in every month of the official season.

## Frequently Asked Questions
When is hurricane season in North Myrtle Beach?+  
The Atlantic Hurricane Season officially runs from June 1 through November 30. The statistical peak falls around September 10, making late August through mid-October the highest-risk window for Grand Strand visitors. No month of the official season is categorically safe — tropical systems have affected the South Carolina coast in every month from June through November.
What are the hurricane evacuation zones in Horry County?+  
Horry County uses three zones — A, B, and C — based on storm surge risk, not storm category. Zone A covers the highest-risk oceanfront and near-ocean areas. Zones B and C extend progressively inland. These zones differ from FEMA flood zone designations. Look up your rental address at scemd.org/prepare/know-your-zone before your trip.
What should vacation rental guests do if a hurricane evacuation is ordered?+  
Leave. Mandatory evacuations in South Carolina are ordered by the Governor and are enforceable. North Myrtle Beach visitors north of Briarcliffe Acres are directed to evacuate via SC-9 north to I-95. Leave early — roads fill quickly. Keep your rental car fueled throughout your stay. Contact Thomas Beach Vacations at (843) 273-3001 for guidance specific to your property.
Does travel insurance cover hurricane evacuations at the beach?+  
Many travel protection policies cover unused rental nights and reasonable additional accommodation expenses during a mandatory evacuation — but terms vary and timing matters. Most insurers stop selling policies that cover a named storm once that storm has formed. Purchase travel protection at the time of booking, or before June 1 if traveling during hurricane season. Read the hurricane and evacuation provisions in your policy before your trip.
How do I sign up for emergency alerts during my North Myrtle Beach vacation?+  
Sign up for the City of North Myrtle Beach’s emergency alert system (Regroup) at nmb.us/705/Alerts using your temporary rental address. Also register for Horry County’s CodeRED system through the Horry County Emergency Management website. Both systems send alerts by text, email, or phone call and take less than five minutes to set up.

# Hurricane Hazel Photograph Collection | Horry County Archives Center | Coastal Carolina University
## Hurricane Hazel Photograph Collection
This collection contains 30 photographs taken in the North Myrtle Beach area in the days immediately after Hurricane Hazel, a Category 4 Hurricane, made landfall on the northeastern coast of Horry County, South Carolina (Ocean Drive section of what is now North Myrtle Beach) on the morning of October 15, 1954.
There were 273 houses destroyed in Myrtle Beach, 120 destroyed at Windy Hill, 200 lost in Crescent Beach, 450 destroyed at Ocean Drive and 300 at Cherry Grove Beach.
For information about the use or reproduction of these images contact the Horry County Museum.
Printing is not supported at the primary Gallery Thumbnail page. Please first navigate to a specific Image before printing.

(WPDE) — Now that we enter October, the seasons are slowly changing and there are only two months left of hurricane season. However, the most active period of hurricane season runs from late August to mid-October, so it's important to stay vigilant.
In fact, while October hurricanes are rare for the Grand Strand, they can be very strong. Since 1851, there have been four hurricanes to move through the Grand Strand within 50 miles of Myrtle Beach.
**LIST: Helene relief donation drop-off sites along Grand Strand**
The first hurricane on record to impact the Grand Strand in October was Hurricane Number 9, which made landfall near Charleston in 1893. Number 9 moved up through Georgetown and Horry counties, on into the Border Belt, and brought wind speeds of 120 miles per hour to Myrtle Beach. This occurred on October 13.
Next was six years later on Halloween, which is why it is referred to as the Halloween Hurricane of 1899. This Category 2 storm made landfall just south of Myrtle Beach with winds of 105 miles per hour. The Halloween Hurricane is the latest hurricane to make landfall in South Carolina in hurricane season since record-keeping began.
The Grand Strand has seen very few October hurricanes, but the ones that have moved through were extremely impactful. The most impactful was Hazel.
Quite some time passed between the Halloween Hurricane and Hurricane Hazel. Hazel made landfall in 1954 as a dangerous, Category 4 storm. Hazel is the benchmark hurricane for the Grand Strand as it destroyed 90% of oceanfront property from Pawleys Island to Little River. Hazel came ashore near Little River with 140 mile-per-hour winds.

There are many accounts throughout the centuries of various storms and hurricanes that have ravaged South Carolina and Myrtle Beach. A brief histroy of these instances is detailed below.
* * *
In**September 1686**a squall that slammed ashore on the South Carolina coast, near present-day Myrtle Beach, was described as: “wonderfully horrid and destructive… Corne is all beaten down and lyes rotting on the ground… Aboundance of our hoggs and Cattle were killed in the Tempest by the falls of Trees.” On the upside, the 1686 storm foiled a Spanish attack on Charles Town by destroying a galley and killing the commander. As they say, every cloud has a silver lining! In that colonial agrarian culture, crops were due to be harvested during the late-summer storm season, hogs were slated for the slaughter, and fall fishing was the backbone of the local economy. If you survived a so-called “September gale,” your next challenge would be to survive the winter.
**In 1700**, “a dreadful hurricane happened at Charles Town which did great damage and threatened the total destruction of the Town, the lands on which it is built being low and level and not many feet above high water mark. The swelling sea rushed in with amazing impetuosity and obliged the inhabitants to fly to shelter.” A ship out of Glasgow, the Rising Sun, had just arrived with a boatload of settlers seeking to make new lives in the New World. It was dashed to splinters in the port with no survivors.
The Withers family was one of the earliest settlers of the area.**In 1822**, a strong hurricane came and blew their house into the ocean, claiming the lives of 18 people inside.
This is the kind of anecdotal evidence that constituted record keeping for centuries, derived from old letters and journals found in trunks stashed away in attics. If a storm stopped in briefly to inflict some minor property damage without decimating crops, destroying livestock and devastating ships at sea, its legacy clearly did not live on. Now that we know hurricanes strike our coast on average once every four years, we can safely assume that whatever early records survive are not telling the whole story.
**Flashing Forward**

On**October 15, 1954**, Hurricane Hazel made landfall on the border between South Carolina and North Carolina as a Category 4 hurricane. Almost 80% of all waterfront dwellings were destroyed during this hurricane and many low-lying barrier islands were completely flooded. This hurricane was particularly devastating and infamous in that the official report from the area Weather Bureau stated: “all traces of civilization on the immediate waterfront between the state line and Cape Fear were practically annihilated.”
On**September 22, 1989**, another Category 4 hurricane made landfall in South Carolina by the name of Hurricane Hugo. This hurricane claimed the lives of 27 South Carolinians and caused extensive waterfront damage, tremendous storm surges and left telephone poles askew and many feet of sand covering roadways. This storm was so severe that at one point, the Weather Bureau reported about 3,000 tornadoes embedded within the hurricane which was to blame for much of the damage.
Over the years, Myrtle Beach has seen several hurricanes come and go and has been fortunate enough to have avoided other devastating storms. The most recent hurricane that came close to Myrtle Beach was Hurricane Irene on**August 23, 2011**. Though Irene made landfall further up the North Carolina coast, Myrtle Beach did receive its share of tropical storm-force winds, with branches and older trees falling and some low flooding being some of the worst of the damage.
Throughout the centuries, modern improvements have made forecasting hurricanes much easier, and Myrtle Beach is often spared the brunt of hurricanes, and the everyday weather of Myrtle Beach keeps visitors coming year after year. But from the early storms of centuries ago to the infamous Hazel, to more recent storms like Floyd and Fran, hurricane historians always have an eye on the Grand Strand. Contact us today!

In**September 1686**a squall that slammed ashore on the South Carolina coast, near present-day Myrtle Beach, was described as: “wonderfully horrid and destructive… Corne is all beaten down and lyes rotting on the ground… Aboundance of our hoggs and Cattle were killed in the Tempest by the falls of Trees.” On the upside, the 1686 storm foiled a Spanish attack on Charles Town by destroying a galley and killing the commander. In that colonial agrarian culture, crops were due to be harvested during the late-summer storm season, hogs were slated for the slaughter, and fall fishing was the backbone of the local economy. If you survived a so-called “September gale,” your next challenge would be to survive the winter.
**In 1700**, “a dreadful hurricane happened at Charles Town which did great damage and threatened the total destruction of the Town, the lands on which it is built being low and level and not many feet above high water mark. If a storm stopped in briefly to inflict some minor property damage without decimating crops, destroying livestock and devastating ships at sea, its legacy clearly did not live on.
